case_name: Forged Construction Ltd. v Westurban Developments Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Forged Construction Ltd. v. Westurban
Developments Ltd.,

2019 BCSC 1550

Date: 20190916

Docket:
S181053

Registry: Victoria

Between:

Forged
Construction Ltd.

Appellant
(Plaintiff)

And:

Westurban
Developments Ltd. and

Nursery Hill GP Inc.

Respondents

On Appeal from reasons of a Master of the Supreme Court

of British Columbia, released April 8, 2019.

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Punnett

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Applicant:

M.R.
Mark

Counsel for the Respondents:

A.L.
Faulkner-Killam

Place and Date of Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

July
15, 2019

Place and Date of Judgment:

Victoria,
B.C.

September
16, 2019

[
1
]

The plaintiff appellant
Forged Construction
subcontracted
with the defendant respondent
Westurban
to provide concrete formwork
services on the property of Nursery Hill GP Inc. in View Royal, B.C. The
appellant commenced this
Builder’s Lien
action in February 2018.

[
2
]

The respondent brought an application before
Master Bouck seeking security for costs, a stay of the action pending payment
into court of the security for costs, liberty to apply for further security
after completion of any examinations for discovery, and costs of the
application.

[
3
]

In reasons released on April 8, 2019, the Master
ordered the appellant to pay $20,000 into court as security for costs, ordered
a stay of the action until the security is provided, and granted the respondent
liberty to apply for further security after completion of examinations for
discovery. The Master also granted costs of the application to the respondent
in the cause.

Background

[
4
]

The background facts are summarized by the
Master:

[4]        The defendant Westurban is the general contractor
on a multi-unit residential project located in the View Royal municipality and
known as Nursery Hill. Nursery Hill GP Inc. is the owner of the property on
which the project is being built.

[5]        In or about August, 2017, the plaintiff contracted
with Westurban to provide concrete and related forming services for the
project. The contract did not go as planned and the parties blame each other
for this circumstance. Indeed, much of the affidavit evidence presented on this
application addresses the contractual dispute between the parties.

[6]        The plaintiff says that it was not fully paid for
its services by Westurban and thus registered a builder’s lien on title on
February 9, 2018. In that lien, the plaintiff claims the sum of $568,986.26 for
unpaid work.

[7]        On February 22, 2018, the plaintiff initiated this
action (the “NOCC”). The NOCC was prepared by the principal of the plaintiff,
Mr. Castel Guiterrez, and seeks payment to the plaintiff for outstanding
invoices in the sum of about $571,400. The NOCC pleads some unusual remedies
such as punitive damages and that Westurban issue a “declaration recanting
Libellous and Defamatory comments” about the plaintiff. In their counterclaim,
the defendants claim damages for the delays and rectifications of deficiencies
allegedly caused by the plaintiff. The defendants also say that the plaintiff
failed to pay its own sub-trades and suppliers, resulting in Westurban having
to meet those obligations.

[8]        Shortly after the plaintiff registered its lien
claim, Westurban brought a petition seeking cancellation of the lien in
exchange for certain security being paid into court. Iyer, J. heard the
petition on March 5, 2018. The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Castel
Guiterrez at the hearing. Iyer, J. ordered that the lien be cancelled and the
sum of $143,636.48 stand as security: see
2018 BCSC 2354
. The court found that
there “are significant deficiencies in the work performed” by the plaintiff:
para. 10. The plaintiff was ordered to pay Westurban’s costs of the petition on
Scale B. Westurban did not deliver its bill of costs to
plaintiff until February 8, 2019. The parties have not reached an agreement on
the amount of costs to be paid. Nevertheless, counsel for the plaintiff advises
that the plaintiff has deposited sufficient monies in the law firm’s trust
account to pay the full amount of the Westurban’s bill.

[9]        The plaintiff is an
Alberta based company and presently in good standing with that province’s
corporate registry. The evidence of the company’s financial health is
relatively slim. The company owns no real property. The two motor vehicles
registered to the plaintiff are leased. Mr. Castel Guiterrez deposes that
as of October 16, 2018, the plaintiff held $173,352.42 in a Bank of Montreal
chequing account that is situated in Alberta. In addition, the plaintiff is
said to have accounts receivable in excess of $250,000 as of late November
2018, excluding the amount in issue in this proceeding. The plaintiff appears
to be actively engaging in business on other projects. Mr. Castel Guiterrez
provides a “profit and loss” statement for the period of July 1 to November 27,
2018, showing a gross profit to the plaintiff of $1,262,135.67. The plaintiff
has not proffered as evidence any financial statements prepared by an accountant,
banking records or corporate income tax returns.

[10]      The defendants asserts that the plaintiff is
judgment proof. The principal of Westurban suggests that the profit and loss
statement is inaccurate in many respects and not reflective of industry
standards. The defendants further observe that one of the plaintiff’s
sub-trades on the Nursery Hill project has brought an action in this court
asking for judgment in the sum of $60,000. The plaintiff is defending that
lawsuit and says that Westurban is liable for the sum claimed.

[11]      The plaintiff’s financial circumstances have been
fluid since the application was originally filed.

[12]      According to the Alberta personal property
registry, all of the plaintiff’s assets are subject to a general security
agreement (“GSA") in favour of Merchant Advance Capital (“Merchant”) that
expires on October 3, 2020. The amount of monies advanced to the plaintiff by
Merchant is not in evidence. However, the GSA secures “all present and
after-acquired personal property of [the plaintiff and Mr. Castel Guiterrez]
including, but not limited to, the future debit/credit card receivables of the
debtors”. Mr. Mark submits that such a GSA is typical for any large
construction business given the need for operating capital while awaiting
payment on contracts.

[13]      When the dispute between the parties first arose,
the plaintiff’s assets were subject to a GSA in favour Riviera Finance Inc. of
Texas (“Riviera”). In fact, on or about October 18, 2017, Westurban acceded to
the plaintiff’s request to pay all monies owing under the sub-contract to
Riviera directly. Because of the contractual dispute between the parties,
Riviera was not paid. Thus, on January 18, 2018, Riviera commenced an action
against the plaintiff in the Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta seeking judgment
in the sum of $228,767.45 plus interest and costs. The lawsuit was eventually
resolved, with the plaintiff paying Riviera the sum of $291,913 over a six
month period ending in December 2018. The evidence does not address the precise
source of those funds except that the plaintiff “made payments” to Riviera. The
monies paid to Riviera form part of the plaintiff’s claim against the
defendants.

[14]      The defendants also make allegations about Mr.
Castel Guiterrez’s personal solvency. The allegations are denied but are, in
any event, irrelevant to a determination of the plaintiff’s ability to pay
costs should this action fail.

[15]      The defendants seek
security in the sum of $48,060.25, based on a bill of costs that includes fees
for a 15 day trial.

Grounds of Appeal

[
5
]

The appellant’s grounds for this appeal are:

(a)        The
Master granted the order absent a finding that the defendant Westurban
established a
prima facie
case the plaintiff had insufficient assets to
pay costs.

(b)        The Master
concluded the assets of the plaintiff were at risk of dissipation without
evidence.

Parties’ Positions on Standard
of Review

[
6
]

The parties disagree on the appropriate standard
of review on an appeal from a Master applicable to these grounds of appeal.

[
7
]

The appellant submits:

(a)       a review of a purely interlocutory decision of
a master is a true appeal and the master’s decision is not to be interfered
with unless it is clearly wrong;

(b)       a question of law, a final order or a ruling
that raises questions vital to the final issue are reviewed by way of a
rehearing on the merits based on the records before the master; even where an
exercise of discretion is involved, the judge appealed to may properly
substitute his or her own view for that of the master.

(
Ralph’s
Auto Supply (B.C.) Ltd. v. Ken Ransford Holding Ltd.
,
2011 BCSC 999
at
para.
7
.)

[
8
]

The appellant submits the first ground of appeal
is a question of law and the standard of review is correctness. The appellant
therefore seeks a rehearing on its merits. The appellant submits the standard
of review for the second ground of appeal is whether the decision was clearly
wrong.

[
9
]

The respondent, on the other hand, submits the
appropriate standard of review respecting both grounds of appeal is whether the
Master was clearly wrong. The respondent submits the first ground of appeal is
mischaracterized by the appellant as a question of law. Rather, the respondent
submits that it is a question of fact, is a decision based on the Master’s
assessment, and is an exercise of judicial discretion.

[
10
]

The respondent also relies on
Beta Properties
Ltd. v. 4301 Hastings Development Ltd.
,
2018 BCSC 103
at para.
17
, noting
that an order for security for costs is an interlocutory order of a
discretionary nature, not a final order, and therefore the appropriate standard
of review is whether the Master was clearly wrong.

Discussion of Standard of
Review

[
11
]

There is no disagreement the Master correctly
set out the law. In the first stage of the legal test for security for costs
the Master had to find the respondent

had established a
prima facie

case the appellant had insufficient assets to pay the respondent’s costs if the
appellant’s case failed. This is not in issue. However, the appellant submits
that while the Master correctly set out this first stage of the test, she did
not apply the test to the facts nor determine whether the respondent

had
established a
prima facie
case.

[
12
]

The appellant refers to the Master’s reasons at
paragraph 22 where she found:

What tips the scales in favour of
ordering security for costs here is the evidence, or lack thereof, with respect
to the terms of the plaintiff’s loan and/or GSA with Merchant. The existence,
and indeed particulars, of both the Riviera and Merchant loans could have been
more fully addressed in Mr. Castel Guiterrez’s first responding affidavit.
Even if the plaintiff ultimately proves at trial that Westurban is to blame for
the Riviera collection action, that action raises the
spectre
of
Merchant also calling its loan before this proceeding is concluded. And, based
on the description of the security, Merchant has a priority claim to the
plaintiff’s cash holdings. The monies provided to the plaintiff by Merchant, in
whatever amount that is, might well be intended solely for operating capital.
However,
that fact does not negate the possibility that there will be no cash available
to the plaintiff to pay the defendants costs if this action fails.
[Emphasis
added by Appellant.]

[
13
]

The appellant submits the Master reviewed the
appellant’s exigible assets and concluded that the appellant had not provided
evidence to demonstrate it had sufficient exigible assets to avoid an order for
security without first finding that the respondent

had established a
prima
facie
case. Therefore, the appellant submits in its first ground of appeal
that the Master erred in law by failing to apply the appropriate legal test.

[
14
]

As noted, the respondent submits the
characterization of the first ground of appeal as a question of law is
incorrect; rather, the respondent submits it is a question of fact that is
mischaracterized by the appellant as a question of law.

[
15
]

For the reasons that follow, in my view the
first ground of appeal is not a question of law. It is a question of fact and
the standard of review to be applied is whether the Master was clearly wrong.

[
16
]

The parties agree the standard to be applied to
the second ground of appeal is whether the Master was clearly wrong.

Discussion

First Ground of Appeal

[
17
]

The appellant submits there was no finding by
the Master that the respondent had established a
prima facie
case the
appellant had insufficient assets to pay costs.

[
18
]

As noted, the Master correctly set out the law
and the test for a
prima facie
case. The Master noted the lack of
reliable evidence of the appellant’s financial situation filed in response to
the respondent’s allegations of the appellant’s cash flow problems. The Master
also referred to the lack of evidence or explanation of the general security
agreement (“GSA”) over the appellant’s assets. It is clear from the Master’s
reasons she found that the respondent’s evidence raised concerns respecting the
ability of the appellant to pay costs and that such evidence was sufficient to
establish a
prima facie
case the appellant lacked sufficient assets to
pay costs. As a result, the first stage of the test was satisfied and the
Master applied the law correctly.

[
19
]

For convenience I repeat the Master’s analysis
in paras. 17-22:

[17]      More recently, the court of
appeal has ruled that once the
prima facie
case is met, security is
generally ordered unless the court is satisfied there is no arguable defence:
Ocean Pastures Corporation v. Old Masset Economic Development
Corporation
,
2016 BCCA 12
, citing with approval
Fat
Mel’s Restaurant Ltd. v. Canadian Northern Shield Insurance Company,
1992 CanLII
1475
(B.C.S.C.). [Footnote omitted].

[18]      On an application for security for costs, the court
is essentially determining the solvency of the corporate plaintiff. A
corporation can be deemed solvent even if its only exigible asset is cash as is
the case here:
WestCorp Solutions Ltd.
v. Collins
,
2014 BCSC 1406
. Furthermore, the
ability to pay Riviera the sum of $291,913.08 in a six-month period suggests
that the plaintiff can meet its obligations as they come due. The strength of
the plaintiff’s claim along with the merits of the defendants’ counterclaim are
somewhat neutral factors as the contradictory allegations regarding those
claims can only be resolved at trial. Similarly, absent cross-examination on
the contents of affidavits, I am not prepared to make any negative findings
about a deponent’s credibility. The uncontroverted evidence from Mr. Castel
Guiterrez is that the plaintiff has both ongoing contracts and sufficient cash
on hand to at least pay the defendant’s proposed costs of $48,000.

[19]      The fact that the plaintiff has yet to pay the
costs awarded by Iyer, J. is also a neutral factor. While the costs order was
effective from pronouncement, the amount to be paid by the plaintiff is not yet
determined and could be the subject matter of an assessment before the
registrar.

[20]      I am not persuaded that the plaintiff’s lack of exigible
assets in B.C. favours ordering security for costs given that there is no
particular barrier to enforcing an order of this court in that province.

[21]      Nonetheless, security for costs has been ordered
where the corporation’s ability to pay costs rests solely with ongoing annual
income:
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160
at para
18
. Moreover, it appears that the evidence before the court in [
WestCorp
] included the
corporation’s historical and current financial statements as prepared by an
accountant. As well, the corporation in question held bank accounts within B.C.
and had never been subject to claims for unpaid debt. The court found that
there was “cogent and compelling” evidence of the corporation’s solvency and
thus ability to pay any costs award.

[22]      What tips the scales in
favour of ordering security for costs here is the evidence, or lack thereof,
with respect to the terms of plaintiff’s loan and/or GSA with Merchant. The
existence, and indeed particulars, of both the Riviera and Merchant loans could
have been more fully addressed in Mr. Castel Guiterrez’s first responding
affidavit. Even if the plaintiff ultimately proves that Westurban is to blame
for the Riviera collection action, that action raises the spectre of Merchant
also calling its loan before this proceeding is concluded. And, based on the
description of the security, Merchant has a priority claim to the plaintiff’s
cash holdings. The monies provided to the plaintiff by Merchant, in whatever
amount that is, might well be intended solely for operating capital. However,
that fact does not negate the possibility that there will be no cash available
to the plaintiff to pay the defendants’ costs if this action fails.

[
20
]

As is clear from the above, the Master referred
to a
prima facie
case being required and then reviewed and assessed the
evidence and authorities. In paragraph 22 she found that the loan and/or the
GSA with Merchant meant there was a priority claim to the appellant’s cash
holdings. She then found that the evidence established it was a real
possibility there would be “no cash available to the appellant to pay the respondent’s
costs” if the action fails. The Master clearly found that a
prima facie

case had been made out.

[
21
]

I find the Master applied the law correctly in
finding that a
prima facie
case was made out. She assessed the evidence
and the authorities in reaching that conclusion. In doing so she properly
exercised her discretion.

[
22
]

An argument similar to that of the appellant was
made in
Beta,
also an appeal from a Master’s security for costs order. In

Beta,
the company had cash funds and consulting income, but the Master
concluded in the totality of the circumstances there was a sufficient risk of
dissipation. The appellant in
Beta
argued this was speculation and not a
finding, however Williams J. rejected that submission:

[36]      While the reasons provided
are brief, the fact is that the decision is a discretionary one. She clearly
recognized the issue; she considered the relevant evidence; she applied her
judgment to assess the issue and to reach a decision. To my mind, that is an
accurate description of what the task of deciding the application required her
to do. It was not something that she could know with certainty, and thus the
matter of judgment was necessary. To characterize it as merely speculation
seems to me a somewhat unhelpful denigration of the task.

[
23
]

As in
Beta,
I am satisfied the
appellant’s first ground of appeal is a mischaracterization of the Master’s
actual reasons. It ignores her reasons read in their totality and attempts to
mischaracterize her assessment of the evidence and the exercise of her
discretion as a legal error. I am satisfied the Master’s reasons respond to the
issues before her and the submissions of the parties.

[
24
]

The first ground of appeal fails.

Second Ground of Appeal

[
25
]

The appellant’s second ground of appeal is that
the Master concluded the assets of the appellant were at risk of dissipation
without evidence. The appellant argues this conclusion was inconsistent with
the evidence and “was instead based on mere speculation.” The appellant submits
this decision was “clearly wrong.”

[
26
]

However, the uncontroverted evidence accepted by
the Master established that the appellant had signed a GSA over all of its
assets in favour of Merchant Advance Capital (“Merchant”). The appellant chose
not to provide particulars of its agreement with Merchant.

[
27
]

The respondent relies on
Pixhug Media Inc. v.
Steeves
,
2016 BCSC 1714
. At para. 93, Pearlman J. concluded that when cash
assets are encumbered by a GSA, a
prima facie
case that the plaintiff
has no exigible assets is established.

[
28
]

The appellant relies on
WestCorp Solutions
Ltd. v. Collins
,
2014 BCSC 1606
and
New Home Warranty of B.C. v. 462146
B.C. Ltd
.,
2000 BCSC 143
. These authorities are both factually
distinguishable from the present case, given that no security for costs was
ordered. In
WestCorp
no GSA was in place and the court found
WestCorp

had sufficient unencumbered assets, no history of claims against it, and
was profitable. In
New Home
the Court was persuaded the plaintiff had
sufficient assets to satisfy any costs claimed. These authorities do provide
that once a defendant establishes a
prima facie
case that the plaintiff
lacks sufficient assets to pay an order for costs, the plaintiff must provide
evidence of exigible assets.

[
29
]

As noted by the Master, the appellant failed to
provide evidence to rebut the
prima facie
case against it. The Master
was satisfied the appellant’s assets were encumbered by a GSA and that in all
of the circumstances an order for security for costs was appropriate.

[
30
]

The Master assessed the evidence under the
applicable legal principles and exercised her discretion judicially. I cannot
say her conclusion was wrong. Indeed, I find no error by the Master in her
findings respecting the risk of the appellant’s funds not being available to
pay the respondent’s costs if the appellant’s action fails.

[
31
]

The second ground of appeal fails.

[
32
]

The appeal is dismissed. Costs of the appeal are
payable to the respondent in the cause.

“The
Honourable Mr. Justice Punnett”
